eu_ai_act_overview.title: The EU AI Act at a glance
eu_ai_act_overview.content: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the world's first comprehensive, horizontal legal framework for artificial intelligence. It follows a risk-based approach: AI systems are sorted into four tiers. Unacceptable-risk systems (for example social scoring by public authorities) are banned outright. High-risk systems are subject to strict requirements such as risk management, data governance, human oversight, logging and conformity assessment. Limited-risk systems carry transparency duties, for example disclosing that content is AI-generated. Minimal-risk systems face no new obligations. A separate chapter regulates general-purpose AI (GPAI) models: large models, such as LLMs, that can serve many downstream applications. Providers of GPAI models face documentation and transparency duties, with stricter obligations for models classified as posing systemic risk. Enforcement lies with national authorities and the newly created European AI Office. Penalties can reach 35 million euros or 7 percent of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.

gpai_obligations.title: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
gpai_obligations.content: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models under the EU AI Act. Article 53 sets four baseline duties for every GPAI provider: (1) draw up and keep up to date technical documentation of the model, including its training and testing process and the results of its evaluation; (2) provide information and documentation to downstream providers who integrate the model into their own AI systems, so that they can meet their own obligations; (3) put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law, in particular the text-and-data-mining opt-out; and (4) publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training the model, using the template provided by the AI Office. Free and open-source models are exempt from duties (1) and (2) unless they pose systemic risk. Article 55 adds duties for GPAI models with systemic risk: perform state-of-the-art model evaluations, including adversarial testing (red-teaming); assess and mitigate possible systemic risks at Union level; track, document and report serious incidents to the AI Office without undue delay; and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. The GPAI obligations became applicable on 2 August 2025, twelve months after the Act entered into force.

systemic_risk_threshold.title: When does a GPAI model pose systemic risk?
systemic_risk_threshold.content: Under Article 51 of the EU AI Act, a general-purpose AI model is presumed to pose systemic risk when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations (FLOPs). The European Commission can also designate a model as posing systemic risk based on the criteria in Annex XIII, which include the number of parameters, the size of the training dataset, and the model's reach among business users in the Union. The Commission may update the FLOP threshold by delegated act to keep pace with technological change. Providers whose models meet the threshold must notify the Commission within two weeks.

ai_act_timeline.title: Timeline: when the EU AI Act applies
ai_act_timeline.content: The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024. Its provisions apply in stages. Prohibitions on unacceptable-risk practices apply from 2 February 2025. Obligations for general-purpose AI models apply from 2 August 2025. Most requirements for high-risk AI systems apply from 2 August 2026, with an extended transition until 2 August 2027 for high-risk AI embedded in products that are already covered by other EU product legislation. GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until 2 August 2027 to comply.

us_executive_order.title: US Executive Order 14110 on AI — and how it compares to the EU
us_executive_order.content: United States Executive Order 14110 on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (October 2023) directed federal agencies to develop AI safety standards, required developers of the most powerful dual-use foundation models to share safety test results with the government under the Defense Production Act, and tasked NIST with producing red-teaming guidance. Unlike the EU AI Act, the US approach relies on executive action and sectoral agencies rather than a single horizontal statute. Observers often compare the EU's binding, risk-tiered obligations for general-purpose AI models with the more voluntary, standards-driven US framework, and debate which approach better balances innovation and safety. The order was rescinded in January 2025, after which US federal AI policy shifted direction again, further widening the gap between the two regimes.

pasta_carbonara.title: Classic Roman pasta carbonara
pasta_carbonara.content: Classic Roman carbonara uses guanciale, eggs, pecorino romano and black pepper. There is no cream in a traditional carbonara. Render the guanciale slowly, whisk yolks with grated pecorino, and combine off the heat so the eggs thicken without scrambling. Reserve a cup of starchy pasta water to loosen the sauce. Spaghetti or rigatoni both work well.
